newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND SEEN ON ROUTE TO UPGRADE IN NEXT S&P RATING.
newsitem.headline: POLAND SEEN ON ROUTE TO UPGRADE IN NEXT S&P RATING.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Corp. has kept Poland's ratings on hold ahead of this year's parliamentary polls, but analysts say the revision of the country's outlook to positive from stable hints an upgrade could be in the works.

Standard & Poor's announced in New York on Tuesday that it affirmed Poland's triple-'B'-minus long-term foreign currency rating and its single-'A'-minus long-term local currency rating and revised the outlook on ratings to positive from stable.

"The next step is for Poland to move to a single 'A' rating possibly after parliamentary polls or in 1998, rather than this year," said David Mars, Director of Emerging Europe and Africa Economic Research at SBC Warburg in London.
Analysts said that despite expectations of an upgrade this time around, analysts were not disappointed by the steady ratings and did not expect investors to change views on Poland.

"The rating reaffirms what has already been known and certainly will not change investor outlook, it is understable that ratings would not change ahead of general elections," said Daniel Schultz, analyst at Societe Generale in London.

Parliamentary polls, due in September, are likely to pit the ruling ex-comminist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) against opposition Solidarity Election Action (AWS) alliance of parties grouped around the country's largest trade union.

"Assuming that a stable government of some form takes power after the elections and that the current account deficit is not proven to be a real danger, the next move will obviously be an upgrade," SBC Warburg's Mars said.

Poland currently also has a BBB rating from IBCA and Baa3 from Moody's. This year's budget law allows Poland to issue $500 million worth of bonds abroad and the finance ministry was expected to issue a Yankee-bond in late June or early July.

Analysts said that although Poland's current account deficit soared to $1.5 billion in the first quarter of 1997 against a $1.3 billion gap in all of 1996, the structure of imports remained investment, not consumer goods oriented.

"Consumer good imports constitute only a small part of Polish imports, they are a natural phenomenon for an emerging economy and keep a lid on inflation," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, head analyst at the government's Centre for Strategic Studies.
Standard & Poor's also affirmed the 'A-1' short-term local currency rating and assigned the 'A-3' short-term foreign currency rating.
The agency said factors behind its decision included prospects for inflation to sink to about 13-14 percent by the end of 1997 from 15.3 in April and to single-digits in 1998.

Analysts said even thought the Polish currency was temporarily weakened by the recent crisis in Czech financial markets, this should not weigh on the assessment of the Polish economy as a whole because of its stronger fundementals.
Analysts said the Czech Republic, whose sovereign debt has an 'A' investment-grade rating from Standard & Poor's, may even be over-rated in comparison to Poland.

"In the Czech-Polish comparison, one country is rated too high in comparison to the other and I think it's the Czech's," SBC Warburg's Mars said, adding that he doesn't think that the Czech Republic's ratings would be reduced in the near future.

Late on Tuesday Wieslaw Szczuka, director of the foreign department in Poland's finance ministry, said the rating showed that the country was heading toward an investment grade, but declined to say when such an upgrade could take place.

"We are pleased with this modification and consider that every positive change is good, even if it takes place in small steps...(it) means that we are perceived rather better than a year ago and we have a chance of an improvement of the rating in future," Szczuka told Reuters.
